title: The Evening Brief: Judge returns, Belichick investigated, LIV files bankruptcy
dek: Tuesday delivered convergence across four sports: Aaron Judge reinstated and set to play Wednesday, Bill Belichick declining comment as UNC's investigation widens, the SEC scheduling Thursday's vote to expel LSU, and LIV Golf filing Chapter 11 bankruptcy after Saudi PIF ended funding.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Tuesday's dominant thread is institutional claims meeting unresolved scrutiny: Belichick maintains compliance while investigators question staff about drug use and inappropriate relationships; the SEC moves toward expulsion despite legal barriers; Judge returns after three months out to a team that went 45-39 without him; and LIV enters bankruptcy with liabilities five to ten times its remaining assets.
bottom_line: Tuesday converged four institutional stress tests: Belichick maintaining compliance while investigations widen, the SEC voting Thursday on LSU expulsion despite legal barriers, Judge returning to a Yankees team that faltered in his absence, and LIV entering bankruptcy with liabilities dwarfing remaining assets. The common thread across sports was the gap between what programs and organizations claim to maintain and what investigations, litigation, and financial crisis will actually allow them to perform. Watch the SEC vote Thursday, the investigation's continuing timeline at UNC, Judge's performance Wednesday and whether he avoids re-injury, and whether LIV's bankruptcy court and financing clearances allow the league to restructure or force liquidation.
body: The day's central pressure point ran through college football and professional sports alike: what programs and leagues claim to maintain versus what investigations, legal action, and financial crisis will actually allow them to perform in real time. Belichick faced his ninth consecutive day of questions about UNC's deepening investigation, offering only that he understood the importance of the investigative team's work and that his program maintains an atmosphere of compliance. General manager Michael Lombardi resigned on September 3 after being placed on leave in late July, and the investigation has expanded to include questions about alleged drug use by coaching staff and inappropriate relationships involving assistant coaches and recruiting staff. Defensive coordinator Steve Belichick, the head coach's son, remains on medical leave. His contract mandates he promote an atmosphere of compliance; the reporting does not state what, if anything, his claims and the investigation's scope will resolve or when.

The SEC's legal battle with LSU escalated Tuesday when the conference filed an amended federal complaint seeking court declaration of the power to expel the school and scheduled a presidential vote for Thursday, September 10. SEC bylaws require a two-thirds majority to expel a member. The filing adds LSU board members and Louisiana attorney general Liz Murrill as defendants and requests a temporary restraining order to prevent LSU from blocking the meeting. A Louisiana state court had issued a prior injunction against SEC enforcement of penalties, creating legal uncertainty about whether the conference can carry out expulsion even if the vote passes. The action follows months of dispute over LSU's recruitment of former NFL players.

In baseball, Aaron Judge was reinstated from the 60-day injured list Monday and is expected to play Tuesday against Colorado, ending a three-month absence from a right rib stress fracture sustained April 26. The Yankees were 36-23 when Judge last played on May 31; through Sunday they were 45-39 without him. Judge declined a Minor League rehab assignment, saying he did not see a point to wasting at-bats. Manager Aaron Boone indicated Judge may play five to seven innings initially and will be encouraged to avoid diving to prevent re-injury. Judge's debut performance and whether he can complete full games will shape the Yankees' offensive trajectory in the final month.

LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in New Jersey federal court Monday after Saudi PIF ended its funding. The league reports liabilities between $500 million and $1 billion against assets between $100 million and $500 million. Saudi PIF committed $49.6 million in debtor-in-possession financing to allow operations during bankruptcy proceedings, a sum representing less than ten percent of LIV's estimated liabilities. The league plans to transition to player-majority ownership. Bankruptcy court approval and BC Partners' exit financing decisions are the next gates for the league's survival.

College football absorbed opening-week injuries that will test program depth through September. Notre Dame lost safety Brauntae Johnson and defensive tackle Jason Onye to lower left leg injuries in the third quarter of a 41-13 victory over Wisconsin on September 6; both wore protective boots on their left feet. Coach Marcus Freeman ruled both out for the remainder of the game but provided no diagnosis or return timeline, saying he would meet with medical staff Monday to assess status for Saturday's game against Rice. Johnson, a junior, recorded four interceptions last season; Onye, a sixth-year senior, started nine games in 2025. Washington lost starting running back Quaid Carr and backup Jayden Limar to injuries in the Apple Cup win over Washington State on September 7. Carr sustained a hand injury requiring surgery; Limar sustained an elbow injury. Coach Jedd Fisch indicated neither will return for several weeks but declined to rule out season-ending status.

On the professional calendar, the New England Patriots signed cornerback Christian Gonzalez to a four-year, $135 million extension with $102 million guaranteed on Monday, making him the NFL's highest-paid cornerback at $33.75 million average annual value. The deal surpasses Devon Witherspoon's $33 million average with Seattle. Gonzalez has played only 34 regular-season games and sustained a lower leg injury in August; the Patriots face Seattle on Wednesday in their season opener. Baker Mayfield signed a three-year, $165 million extension with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Monday, averaging $55 million per year and resolving a training-camp holdout. The deal locks Mayfield through 2029 and places him in the elite quarterback salary tier. The Buccaneers open at Cincinnati on September 15.

College football's opening weekend results showed the MAC appealing Michigan's 13-12 victory over Western Michigan, filed Tuesday to the NCAA FBS Oversight Committee and College Football Playoff. The MAC argues the Big Ten replay crew violated established protocol by relying on the clock embedded in its replay system rather than the game clock displayed on the program feed, resulting in one second being restored and an additional play awarded to Michigan. The established protocol requires use of the program feed clock. The MAC's appeal faces NCAA rules stating a final score is final once declared. The cricket franchise landscape shifted when Cricket Australia approved Big Bash League privatization, moving forward with a sales process for the Melbourne Renegades with a target date of the 2027-28 season for new ownership. Cricket Australia adopted a self-determination model allowing individual states to choose whether and when to sell stakes in their franchises, retreating from an earlier proposal for league-wide privatization after opposition from New South Wales and Queensland.

Tennis saw Zheng Qinwen defeat Iga Swiatek 7-5, 6-3 in the US Open fourth round on September 7, erasing a 5-0 first-set deficit. The victory marks the second consecutive match in which Zheng won seven games in a row from 0-5 down, against two Grand Slam champions. A player winning seven games from 0-5 down in consecutive sets against two different Grand Slam winners has never happened before at the highest level. Zheng faces second seed Elena Rybakina in the quarterfinals.
